items.title: The cost of basics keeps rising but 'anti-fascist economics' could lower them
paras: Isabella Weber, an associate professor of economics, says the soaring cost of essentials is severely testing democracies.
In a new book, she says policymakers need to make affordability the centre of "anti-fascist economics".
Dr Weber says it will require "structuralist measures" that change the ways in which we provision the essentials in society.
Isabella Weber, a rising-star German economist, says it is something we need to pursue again.
She says fascism has made a comeback. Our economic and political systems have stopped making our lives better and people are furious about it.

She says illiberal forces are exploiting voters' anger and, rather than addressing the material causes of their pain, are deliberately redirecting people's rage towards migrants and other minorities, and promising that salvation can be found in nationalism, ethnic purity or patriarchy.

To combat the phenomenon, she argues, we have to make life's essentials affordable again — housing, food, energy, water, health care, transport — so the foundations for a dignified life are available to everyone, no matter your household income or class.
"It's funny that today we think of anti-fascist economics as provocative," she told the ABC Business Daily podcast .
"In the 1940s it was actually a mainstream point for economists to say that economics had a role to play in 'Never Again'.
"I would argue that today we are [once again] in a deep crisis of democracy around the Western world. The extreme right is on the rise. Democracy is as unstable as it has been since the 40s.
"I think people are very clear. They're saying they can't take the status quo anymore," she said.
Isabella Weber speaks to the ABC about her new book, Anti-Fascist Economics. ( ABC News )
Dr Weber, an associate professor of economics at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, shot to prominence (or notoriety) in December 2021.

She published an op-ed in The Guardian arguing that, in the wake of the COVID lockdowns, it could be worth using temporary and strategic price controls on certain products to prevent large companies in systemically significant sectors from exploiting the chaos to make windfall profits (and sending higher prices through the system).

She said they were a standard tool of economic management in the 1940s. They had been used to prevent inflation spiking dangerously in the transitional years when warfare economies were shifting back from a supply-constrained world with pent-up consumer demand (and high household savings) to post-war peacetime economies when domestic supply had recovered.
She saw strong parallels between the two historical periods. But the fallout from her article was immediate.

"In a matter of hours, Weber, who was 33 years old, had transformed from an obscure but respected academic … into the most hated woman in economics — simply for proposing a 'serious conversation about strategic price controls'," Zach Carter wrote in The New Yorker .
Weber agrees that her article "touched a nerve deep inside the economics establishment".
"The idea that targeted price controls as an emergency measure merit serious consideration was greeted as if I had recommended a pornography exhibition in the Vatican," she writes in her book.

"[But] for months, in public earnings calls with their shareholders, corporate leaders had been gleefully celebrating the fact that the pandemic, spiking commodity prices, and supply chain dislocations provided a wonderful opportunity to jack up prices.

"As my co-authors and I later showed with research powered by large-language models analysing 138,962 earnings calls, corporate leaders tend to talk positively about generalised cost shocks, which impact workers and households negatively, because they are good for pricing and the bottom line."
Jump forward to 2026, and Weber says the high inflation that so many countries are still experiencing is one big problem among many.

She says it is adding to the pressure-cooker environment that millions of people have been living in for decades, where the costs of basic essentials such as housing, food, energy and health have been rising much faster than prices of non-essentials such as TVs, electronics and toys.
The graphic below shows what happened to the price of essentials and non-essentials in the United States between 2000 and 2022. When it was published a few years ago it went viral on the internet.
( Supplied: Nick Routley, Visual Capitalist, Consumer price inflation, by type of good or service (2000-2022), February 22, 2023 )
It illuminates a point Dr Weber is making about the drivers of inequality under neoliberal capitalism.
She says when people living in the richest countries in the world are still struggling to pay for basics it is unsurprising why they are so angry.

In her book, she argues that modern scarcities in basic public services and housing are the outgrowth of decades of austerity and "market subordination at all costs" and that that scarcity has become "the breeding ground of hate".
"Price shocks in essentials are always simultaneously inequality shocks," she writes.
"Usually we only consider income dynamics like wage stagnation as the driver of inequality increases … [but] price increases in essentials can be of similar importance."
In the book, she explains that anti-fascist economics is not her idea. It used to be commonplace.
Karl Polanyi, the Austrian émigré scholar who theorised about fascism in the 1930s and 1940s (and from which he had to flee to London) was one economist who wrote about it in detail.

She told the ABC that "anti-fascist economics" would improve peoples' lives, and rebuild their faith in democracy, by securing and delivering the necessities for people at affordable prices and with their affordability safeguarded.

Dr Weber says we have levels of corporate concentration today, including in essential sectors, where a handful of companies have control over the things that people and industry can not do without, and that is a problem that needs addressing.
"In the 1940s [it] actually was one of the arguments that economists made that, you know, whoever controls the essentials has quite a considerable degree of control over [an] economy and society.
"And as such, in a democracy, we have to ask the question of how we organise the essentials."
"But it's also a question of, you know, whose interests are political representatives actually standing up for?

"Under neoliberalism, we have been telling people for decades that democracy is the greatest of all political systems, which of course it is, but at the same time, even when it comes to the most basic things you need for a dignified life, 'There's not much that the elected representatives can do for you.'

"Anti-fascist economics is about creating an economic policy playbook that addresses the essentials, makes them affordable with short-run measures, and then introduces more structuralist measures that change the ways in which we provision the essentials."

items.title: Oil, smoke and Myanmar: The key issues facing South-East Asia
paras: Jeepney drivers, a critical part of the Philippines' transportation system, protest the high fuel prices prompted by the war in the Middle East ahead of the ASEAN summit. ( Reuters: Eloisa Lopez )
World leaders are in the Philippines today, engaging in a flurry of high-level diplomacy amid a destabilised global order and rising geopolitical tensions.
This year's Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila will set the tone before US President Donald Trump and other leaders head to China for APEC talks.
A meeting of the Quad is also likely; the strategic partnership between India, Japan, Australia and the United States that is seen as a means of checking China's growing influence across Asia.
With numerous global challenges, these issues are set to dominate the ASEAN agenda.
The war in the Middle East is making it much more expensive to refuel in car-centric Manila. ( Reuters: Eloisa Lopez )
The war in Iran and the ensuing chaos in global energy markets are front of mind for leaders, as much of South-East Asia is heavily reliant on oil and gas from the Middle East.
Hunter Marston, South-East Asia program director at the Lowy Institute, said the energy issue has been "massive".
"It's triggered protests … and has caused enormous headaches for political leaders," he said.
"ASEAN this year has been emphasising progress towards a strategic petroleum reserve and the ASEAN power grid.
"These are both signals of the recognition that ASEAN needs to do something to shore up its regional resilience and its ability to withstand external shocks."
Theresa Lazaro is the Philippines' Secretary of Foreign Affairs. ( ABC News: Tim Swanston )
For decades, ASEAN nations have been investigating ways to connect electricity infrastructure across nations to bolster energy security.
Philippines Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro told the ABC that discussions are underway to advance these regional energy resilience projects.
"Of course, it's a very expensive and protracted issue, but I think it's really about time that we have to implement this ASEAN energy grid," she said.
The Philippines has faced repeated incidents over competing territorial claims in the South China Sea. ( AP: Aaron Favila )
While competing territorial claims in the South China Sea have always been a key issue for ASEAN nations, these disputes will hit close to home this year.
The Philippines has experienced numerous maritime confrontations with China over the contested waterway.
China claims almost all of the South China Sea through its "nine-dash line", a claim a tribunal at The Hague found to have no basis under international maritime law a decade ago.
Despite this, China is accused of employing low-level acts of aggression below the threshold of armed conflict, including blasting Philippine Coast Guard vessels and fishing boats with water cannons.
ASEAN has been trying to negotiate a Code of Conduct with China to de-escalate tensions and provide a framework for dealing with disputes.
The Philippines was hopeful it would be finalised by the end of this summit, although that now appears unlikely.
China's claims in the South China Sea cut through the majority of its neighbours' claims. ( ABC News graphic: Jarrod Fankhauser )
Mr Marston wasn't sure if the final code of conduct would reduce tensions or the risk of escalation.
"It's not clear that this will constrain China's behaviour in the South China Sea," he said.
"(But) it has tied ASEAN member states and Beijing together in the process of negotiations."
Mr Marston said the code doesn't hold China "accountable" and China had previously violated the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea despite being one of the first countries to sign up.
Meanwhile, Australia signed a defence agreement with the Philippines this month to further support its coast guard and navy.
Myanmar's military took power following a coup in 2021. ( Reuters: Ann Wang )

More than five years after Myanmar's military junta seized control of the country in a coup, the conflict between the military, pro-democracy resistance groups and ethnic armed organisations continues to rage on.
An estimated 100,000 people have been killed and millions displaced, according to UN officials.
Elections held earlier this year helped junta leader Min Aung Hlaing become president; however, they were widely dismissed by critics as a "sham".
ASEAN adopted a "Five-Point Consensus" shortly after the coup, calling for an end to violence, dialogue, mediation, humanitarian assistance and visits by an envoy.
Despite criticism of the plan's implementation, ASEAN has stuck with it.
Ms Lazaro recently visited Myanmar as an envoy, describing the "situation" as "deplorable".
Aung San Suu Kyi was detained following a coup in 2021. ( Myanmar State TV )
Ms Lazaro didn't meet with former Myanmar leader Aung San Suu Kyi but was told she was "doing well".
The 81-year-old was moved to house arrest earlier this year and was visited by a delegate of the International Committee of the Red Cross.
Myanmar's leader, Min Aung Hlaing, and high-level junta politicians are barred from ASEAN meetings to pressure the military-backed government to implement the Five-Point Consensus.
But analysts believe some ASEAN countries, which have been re-establishing bilateral ties with Myanmar, have been undermining these efforts.
Ms Lazaro said those countries were "just recalibrating their bilateral relationships" rather than undermining the consensus.
The US has also been holding secretive talks with Myanmar, possibly to gain access to its enormous reserves of rare earth metals, pivotal in the manufacturing of modern technologies.
At this year's summit, discussions are underway between ASEAN nations over whether to end the ban on Myanmar's military-backed leaders attending the meetings.
Motorists on the Kahayan Bridge travel through a haze as wildfires shroud the area. ( Reuters: Usep Hariadi )
A Super El Niño weather pattern is in full swing across South-East Asia, projected to peak in late 2026 and early 2027.
The intensity of the weather phenomenon has brought drought, extreme heat and agricultural disruptions across large parts of the region.
In Indonesia, it has underpinned the worst forest and land fire season in more than a decade, worsening underlying conditions as "slash and burn" fires are lit to clear land for plantations.
The fires have at times blanketed large swathes of Indonesia and travelled across borders, covering Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines in toxic smoke.
The smoke has caused diplomatic tensions between Indonesia and Singapore, with Singapore at times among the top 10 most polluted cities by air quality.
It has pushed the ratification of a proposed cross-border haze-pollution authority up the agenda, with Indonesia's neighbours keen to take further action.
Firmus is one of many AI companies investing in countries like Singapore. ( Supplied: Firmus )
This summit also comes amid global public uncertainty over the growing capability of artificial intelligence (AI).
The grouping is expected to sign a digital economy framework, something ASEAN says is the first region-wide digital economy agreement.
ASEAN is projected to become the fourth-largest economic bloc by 2030, with a relatively young population, so how it manages future digital transformation could impact the rest of the world.
This year's ASEAN comes right before APEC, where major AI leaders like the US and China will meet.
Some ASEAN countries, like Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, have seen considerable investment in data centres, which have supported their economies during challenging global economic conditions.
"As far as ASEAN is concerned, I think we look positively on (AI)," Ms Lazaro said.
"President Marcos wanted to really emphasise AI in the very first summit in May, but we were sidelined because of the Middle East Crisis."

US President Donald Trump will reportedly use his visit to ASEAN to press South-East Asian countries to join the US-led 'Pax Silica', an initiative that seeks to reduce the reliance on China in the AI supply chain.

items.title: Coalition threat to sink gas reform triggers rare industry backlash
paras: Advertisement Business Companies Energy Coalition threat to sink gas reform triggers rare industry backlash Nick Toscano November 16, 2026 — 5:00am
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Share A A A A broad alliance of business chiefs and unions has mounted a last-minute push for the Coalition to pass Labor’s domestic gas-reservation laws, warning that scuttling or delaying the scheme will put hundreds of thousands of industrial jobs at risk and inflate household energy bills.

The Senate is due to vote this week on legislation to compel liquefied natural gas shippers to hold back up 20 per cent of their annual export volumes for the local market from 2028. The Albanese government argues this will head off domestic shortfalls and curb the costs of heating, electricity and manufacturing.

Most of Australia’s LNG is produced in Queensland or Western Australia, and is sold on long-term contracts to Asia. Bloomberg However, the bill faces defeat without major amendments. The Coalition has signalled it would not vote for it in its current form, while the Greens have rejected the legislation, demanding a 25 per cent tax on gas exports instead.

In a major intervention, organisations representing heavy manufacturers, petrochemical firms, aluminium smelters and factory workers have signed a joint letter urging senators to back the bill before federal parliament rises for the year.

Acknowledging that they “rarely speak with one voice”, the signatories warned that failing to pass the legislation immediately would deny industry and consumers desperately needed certainty over future gas supplies.
“Delay is not a neutral outcome,” the letter states. “We ask every senator to put the national interest first and pass this bill.”

The government’s proposed reservation scheme aims to address a long-held grievance: that multinational energy giants are earning billions of dollars a year selling LNG to Asia, while local households and factories have faced tightening domestic gas supplies and soaring prices.

Western Australia has long required its LNG exporters to reserve 15 per cent of their production for local use, while Queensland’s export industry was established a decade ago without such rules. The federal scheme would, for the first time, impose reservation rules on the joint ventures that run the three giant LNG export terminals on Queensland’s Curtis Island, operated by Shell, Origin Energy and Santos.

For gas-intensive manufacturing businesses, the reservation would be a long-awaited lifeline. Industry leaders have rallied behind the policy, arguing the domestic gas market is “broken” following a threefold surge in gas prices over the past decade, warning more Australian factories that rely on gas as a feedstock or to fire their kilns and furnaces will be forced to close unless cheaper gas supplies can be secured under long-term contracts.

Without urgent new gas supplies becoming available to help replace rapidly declining domestic gas fields in the Bass Strait, customers in Victoria and NSW could face shortfalls and higher prices by the end of the decade, energy authorities warn.

The joint letter has been backed by Manufacturing Australia – a coalition of 12 of the nation’s biggest manufacturing businesses, such as BlueScope Steel, Dulux Group, Brickworks and Cement Australia – as well as the Australian Industry Group, the Australian Aluminium Council, Chemicals Australia and the Energy Users Association of Australia. Other signatories include the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU), the Australian Manufacturing Workers Union, and the Australian Workers Union.

The letter notes that gas-reservation rules had been recommended by governments of all colours for more than a decade. It urges senators not to let negotiations drag on into next year. “The scheme can and should be refined through development of supporting regulations and through periodic review,” it says.

However, the scheme has sparked pushback from oil and gas industry leaders, many of whom remain concerned about the policy’s design and the risk it could depress domestic prices to the point that investment in new gas fields becomes uneconomic, triggering supply and price shocks in the future.

The industry has also raised alarm over the scheme’s “must-sell” obligation, which would require LNG producers to deliver, not just offer, prescribed volumes to local buyers, raising concerns over uncommercial deals being enforced to meet compliance targets.

Opposition resources spokeswoman Susan McDonald said the Coalition was willing to work with Labor on the scheme to “get this right”, but would not back the bill in its current form. She echoed the gas industry’s warnings that forcing a domestic glut would kill off investment needed to secure future supplies.

“Labor’s proposal in its current form will drive away investment, destroy domestic-only producers, discourage new production and ultimately leave Australians with less gas and higher prices,” she said.

Last week, Ryan Stokes, chair of oil and gas firm Beach Energy, whose top shareholder is the Stokes family’s Seven Group Holdings, said the scheme would not deliver more gas into the system, but would “undercut the companies that have always supplied it”.

Manufacturing Australia chief executive Ben Eade rejected that argument, and delivered a blunt warning to the Coalition that it now had to choose whether to support Australia’s 900,000 manufacturing workers, or the interests or the “commercial interests of three small gas producers” – Beach Energy, Amplitude Energy, and Gina Rinehart-backed Senex Energy – who had been the “loudest voices against the scheme”.
Eade said those gas companies were entitled to put their case but were “not entitled to hold a structural national economic reform to ransom”.
“The Coalition can’t say it backs manufacturing and lower energy bills and then block the only gas reservation scheme before this Parliament,” he said.

items.title: Traditional Aboriginal rock art meets modern style on the world stage
paras: Ivan Namarnyilk paints precise, thin strokes with his manyilk, a traditional brush made of sedge grass. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst )

Sitting at a table in a tiny art gallery nestled inside Kakadu National Park, Blaldja artist Ivan Namarnyilk slowly paints precise, thin strokes with his manyilk, a traditional brush made of sedge grass.
But before Namarnyilk even has the chance to finish his pieces, tourists visiting the Marrawuddi Arts and Culture Centre in Jabiru are asking to buy them.
Ivan Namarnyilk says his art is "like the country, the animals, the people, everything has connection". ( ABC News: Dane Hirst )
Taught by his father, fellow prominent artist Spider Namirrki, at Mudginberri Station, Namarnyilk has been painting "rock art" on paper since he was a teenager.
More than three decades on, Namarnyilk is keeping his culture alive by passing it on to the next generation.
Known for his detailed, x-ray style works, Namarnyilk mainly uses ochre to paint or scratch-draw local animals and cultural totems before applying his signature, mouth-blown clay handprint.
Ivan Namarnyilk’s art uses natural ochres along with his signature hand print. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst )
"We use natural colour like red ochre, white clay, yellow ochre," he says.
"I like painting spirit man, kangaroo, echidna, turtle, fish like barramundi or black bream.
"We respect our totems — my father's totem is irritja [wedge-tailed eagle] and my mother's is duwa [mud crab]."
In August, Namarnyilk sold thousands of dollars worth of his art at his first solo exhibition during the Mahbilil Festival in Jabiru.
Ivan Namarnyilk held his first solo exhibition at the Mahbilil Festival in August. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst )
He says sharing his pieces was "really special" and vital for helping to financially support his family.
Over the past 25 years, more than 500 West Arnhem Indigenous artists have sold pieces at the Marrawuddi Arts and Culture Centre.
Business manager Caron Farrell says the gallery buys artwork "up-front" from about 30 regular makers, with 40 per cent of sales proceeds going towards keeping the centre open.
Caron Farrell says "visitors are quite taken aback to the different styles" on display. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst )
"This space does all of West Arnhem so it's really important for the artists to be able to bring their art here in all different forms," she says.
Ms Farrell says it's a treat for holiday-makers passing through Jabiru to watch the artists paint, scratch, draw and weave onsite, before taking the pieces back to their homes all around the world.
Demand for Ivan Namarnyilk’s pieces has never been higher, with the proceeds helping to support his family and the gallery. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst )
"It's really important for Jabiru to get the tourists in and keep this place going for that art to be in homes," she says.
"I think they get a bit shocked of how much there is and how vast the art is, like [it's] a little bit different say to central desert, the style.
"Obviously, West Arnhem, it's art that you see on all the rock formations, compared to say, central desert, where it's the dot painting.
"You find visitors are quite taken aback to the different styles that are here."

items.title: Worrying signs as Wallabies leave it too late to fire in Scotland defeat
paras: The Wallabies are running out of time, and excuses. ( AP Photo: Scott Heppell )
It might be unfair to be overly critical about the Wallabies' latest defeat, this time to Scotland at Murrayfield.

This was an afternoon of such monochrome dreariness that even Scotland couldn't muster much of their usual attacking verve, dank and grey, the lingering firework smoke above the playing surface reminiscent of some primordial Celtic realm
It was far removed from the bright lights of Friday night in Paris or Saturday afternoon in Cardiff.

Opposing skippers Rory Darge and Harry Wilson both referred to the game as descending into an arm-wrestle, though at times the contest we witnessed was so bad that calling it as such would almost be cruel to practitioners of that maligned pastime.
But then again, autumnal Scottish afternoons are just not what the proponents of free-flowing, attacking rugby union had in mind as ideal conditions for their craft.
Les Kiss said as much to UK broadcaster ITV, describing the game as "turgid".
"I think [Gregor Townsend] and I both would have preferred some drier weather," he added.
Both teams struggled to hold onto the ball in cold and wet conditions. ( Getty Images: David Rogers )

Undoubtedly, the conditions were reflected in the Scottish play as the hosts produced a litany of errors, most of which were a by-product of a series of over-complicated running lines that looked perfect when drawn up in the dryness and warmth of the training rooms, but less so when countered by the freezing rain and fast-pressing Wallabies defence.
The Wallabies had conceded seven tries in each of its previous three games, letting 138 points be scored against them. Shipping just two against Scotland marked a huge improvement.
But neither side hit the attacking heights both are capable of — a familiar failing of this Wallabies team at present.
Where the Scots limitations seemed a result of over complication, the Wallabies' attacking limits were self-imposed by the bland simplicity of their game plan.
Scotland barged their way up to the Wallabies line and spun the ball wide to an unmarked Matt Fagerson to open the scoring.
Matt Fagerson scored the opening try. ( Getty Images: Nations Championship/Ian MacNicol )
The Wallabies went up the other end and hit back immediately, Harry Potter finishing a move started by Carter Gordon's driving surge.

This was what the Wallabies didn't have against England; the fly half taking charge, double-pumping the pass as he approached the line before releasing Jeremy Williams, Len Ikitau and finally Potter to score.
It took the best part of an hour before we saw anything of the like again from the men in gold.

Between times, fans were subject to a dour attacking display whenever the Wallabies had the ball in hand, the visitors relentlessly forced to retreat back up field before either kicking the ball away or flat-out losing it.
One-out runners with no passing, no speed in the back line movement, no width, no use of the thrilling attacking talents at their disposal, no way through the walls of Scottish defenders.
One of the most desperate passages came with about quarter of an hour remaining.

The Wallabies had forced a line out just outside the Scotland 22, a rare attacking chance. But through 18 phases of bland hit ups with little to no imagination the Wallabies went backwards a handful of metres, and then lost the ball to a Scotland turnover.
A kind observation would have been that the Wallabies were being patient, taking their time to find an opening in a Scottish defence that had significantly tightened its leash.
A less kind one would be that it was clueless and uninventive, destined to fail.
The Wallabies struggled to make anything happen with the ball in hand. ( AP Photo: Scott Heppell )
Neither side had anything like clean ball, a litany of errors plaguing the contest in the loose, with the chaotic breakdown simply adding to the confused display from both teams.
But the Wallabies showed they can attack when they want to, adding to the frustration of what had gone before.
Ben Donaldson came onto the field, shifting Gordon to centre and immediately made an impact, passing wide and giving the visitors the impetus to attack.

With almost his first phase of play, Donaldson immediately looked to move the ball wide, moving laterally at pace to open the Scotland defence — perhaps running himself into a starters spot in Cardiff next week.
Later, Donaldson spun the ball wide to Williams, whose flick pass out the back of the hand released Jorgensen to scoot down the line and score.

As the clock ticked into the red, the ball was again spun wide, Tate McDermott and Harry Wilson releasing Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, almost a non-entity both this week and last in an attacking sense but finally running with the ball in hand.
Jorgensen and Tom Wright were both involved before the later was bundled into touch, the gun-shy Wallabies now firing from the hip with alacrity.
Suaalii. Jorgensen. Wright. These names had barely been mentioned all game.
Tom Wright and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii were barely seen in an attacking sense. ( Getty Images: Nations Championship/Ian MacNicol )
Again, perhaps it's unfair to judge the Wallabies too harshly for a sour outing in which both teams struggled to rouse themselves from their mutual stupor.
So attention should shift to Wales, who now awaits inside the Principality Stadium next Sunday (AEDT).
The roof in Cardiff means "conditions" is not an excuse that can be laid down in case of another attacking no-show.
But Wales's defence may yet be just as stingy as it was against the All Blacks, where the Welsh made a stunning 346 tackles.
For reference, Scotland (154) and the Wallabies (194) combined to make 348 at Murrayfield.
The Wallabies have one more chance to prove they are moving in the right direction.
They would do well to find a way to unleash their attacking weapons before it's too late.

items.title: Reserve Bank of India imposes monetary penalty on One Mobikwik Systems Limited
paras: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has, by an order dated November 06, 2026, imposed a monetary penalty of ₹9.00 lakh (Rupees Nine Lakh only) on One Mobikwik Systems Limited (the company) for non-compliance with certain provisions of the directions issued by RBI on ‘Prepaid Payment lnstruments (PPIs)’ and ‘Fraud reporting’. This penalty has been imposed in exercise of powers conferred on RBI under the provisions of section 30(1) read with section 26(6) of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. The statutory inspection of the company was conducted by RBI with reference to its operations for the period from June 2025 to March 2026. Based on supervisory findings of non-compliance with RBI directions and related correspondence in that regard, a notice was issued to the company advising it to show cause as to why penalty should not be imposed on it for its failure to comply with the said RBI directions. After considering the company’s reply to the notice, additional submissions made by it and oral submissions made during the personal hearing, RBI found that the following charges against the company were sustained, warranting imposition of monetary penalty: the company had allowed fund transfer by certain PPI holders to non-pre-registered beneficiaries beyond the prescribed limit. the company failed to report certain frauds within the prescribed timeline. The action is based on deficiencies in regulatory compliance and is not intended to pronounce upon the validity of any transaction or agreement entered into by the company with its customers. Further, imposition of monetary penalty is without prejudice to any other action that may be initiated by RBI against the company. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1496

items.title: ED arrests six persons in cross-border drugs smuggling network
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): The Enforcement Directorate ( ED ) has arrested six persons in connection with an investigation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) case linked to a cross-border drug smuggling network, the agency said on Tuesday. ED 's Delhi unit arrested these accused in different operations launched on October 11, October 18 and October 20. The arrested accused are identified as Lovejit Singh alias Labba, Manjeet Singh alias Manna, Prabhjit Singh, Gurjot Singh, Ramandeep Singh, and Gurpreet Singh. "A major drug trafficking operation involving smuggling of heroin from Afghanistan into India was unearthed during investigation," said the ED in a statement. The PMLA investigation was initiated on the basis of seizure of 293.81 kg of heroin from containers imported by Sandhu Exports at Nhava Sheva Port by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence and seizure of 352.71 kg of heroin from two vehicles and a flat in Faridabad, Haryana, by the Delhi Police Special Cell. Thus, a total of 646.52 kg of heroin has been seized so far. ED investigation revealed that the arrested persons, Lovejit Singh, Manjeet Singh, Ramandeep Singh, Gurjot Singh, Gurpreet Singh and Prabhjit Singh, coordinated the smuggling, storage and distribution of heroin across Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi.

"These individuals were key members of a syndicate that smuggled heroin from Afghanistan and Iran, concealing them within shipments of talc stone and gypsum powder," said the ED . Accused persons incorporated Sandhu Exports, a front company owned by Prabhjit Singh, to carry out the smuggling of drugs, informed the federal agency. ED uncovered the highly sophisticated heroin smuggling and money laundering network where identification of multiple bank accounts, cash transactions, and operational expenses by the accused has been made. "Accused disguised the origin of the illicit funds, which were further layered and integrated into seemingly legitimate financial activities. It was also revealed that the syndicate did not make any payments to Afghan suppliers until the drugs were sold in local markets." Further, the agency said the accused used cash payments to purchase multiple vehicles including Toyota Fortuner, Etios and Hyundai Verna etc in second hand market for trafficking from the storage Hubs to further distribution. The ED investigation revealed that cash was used for the purchase of high-end smartphones and encrypted communication apps were used to coordinate smuggling activities. "Drugs smuggled from Iran and Afghanistan used to be imported via the Nava Sheva port in Mumbai, later stored at a rented godown in Shivpuri, Madhya Pradesh and further distributed for local supply in parts of Delhi, Punjab and Haryana. Transportation was carried out in lesser quantities of 10 kg to prevent detection by law enforcement agencies. Earlier, a property in Jandoli Village (Rajpura, Punjab), multiple bank accounts in the names of accused persons, and fixed deposits have been attached by ED ," added the agency. (ANI)

items.title: Asia's Largest Mindfulness India Summit 2024 Marks a New Era for Corporate Culture and Personal Well-being with the Inau
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel PNN Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: The Mindfulness India Summit 2024, an initiative by the Mindful Science Centre, presented by HSBC and supported by CII Leadership and HR Committee, successfully concluded its two-day event on October 17 and 18, 2024, establishing new benchmarks in corporate culture and personal well-being. With over 40 international and national experts addressing mindfulness, emotional intelligence, and neuroscience, the summit highlighted how these principles are essential in transforming leadership, enhancing employee engagement, and fostering sustainable well-being within organizations. The evolving workplace landscape, particularly the increasing role of AI, requires a renewed focus on human-centric leadership and emotional resilience. The summit provided a platform for forward-thinking leaders to explore how mindfulness can effectively bridge this gap, ensuring both corporate excellence and employee well-being . The summit featured MasterChef Sanjeev Kapoor as the Chief Guest, who shared how mindful leadership has played a pivotal role in building his culinary empire. Along with Chris Ruane, Ex MP British Parliament and Chair of Mindfulness Initiative UK, J N Behl and Global Holistic Health Guru Mickey Mehta, Kapoor also launched Manish Behl's new book "Observe - 101 Mindfulness Practices", a guide designed to make mindfulness accessible for both professionals and individuals in their everyday lives. Behl, a global mindfulness expert and founder of the Mindful Science Centre, shared, "With this book, I want to demystify mindfulness and make it accessible to everyone. Mindfulness is not a complex or distant concept, but a practical tool for reducing stress, improving focus, and fostering deeper connections in both personal and professional settings." The Mindfulness India Summit 2024 has successfully proven that mindfulness is no longer a luxury but a necessity in modern corporate structures. By adopting mindfulness practices, organizations are not only creating more compassionate work environments but are also enhancing their overall performance and sustainability in a world increasingly shaped by technological and emotional complexity. The 2 days also saw the launch of Mindfulness Impact Awards, to honor organizations and individuals who have integrated mindfulness into their corporate structures and personal lives. These awards reflect the growing recognition that workplace culture directly affects employee productivity, creativity, and overall well-being. Manish Behl, founder of the awards, explained, "Corporate success today goes beyond profit; it's about fostering environments where employees thrive mentally, emotionally, and physically. Our vision with these awards is to inspire a deeper integration of mindfulness in corporate cultures worldwide. By recognizing these pioneers, we hope these awards inspire companies and individuals to further integrate mindfulness into their environments, ultimately fostering happier, more productive workplaces, communities, and a more compassionate world." The awards were designed to acknowledge champions of mindfulness across categories, recognizing those who incorporate mindful practices to improve workplace culture, employee engagement, and societal impact. Winners ranged from corporate giants like Aditya Birla Group and Accenture to global educators and community leaders. items.title: Indian students in Kazan delighted as PM Modi arrives for BRICS Summit
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Kazan [ Russia ], October 22 (ANI): Indian students in Kazan , Russia , are happy and excited about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's arrival at Hotel Korston , as he attends the 16th BRICS Summit . Notably, PM Narendra Modi on Tuesday touched down in Kazan city of Russia to participate in the 16th BRICS Summit and received a warm welcome. He is here to attend the 16th BRICS Summit , being held under the Chairmanship of Russia . To welcome PM Modi , students from India studying in Russia also sang a welcome song as they awaited PM Modi 's arrival at Hotel Korston . An Indian student from Pune, Saniya said that the students are quite excited to greet PM Modi . "Maybe we will get the opportunity (to meet PM Modi ) as many students are here (at Hotel Korston )... We are very excited. We are lucky to have this opportunity and we are happy to see him," she told ANI. An Indian student from Bihar, Shaurya Pratap said, "We are very happy to welcome PM Modi and we have prepared a song for him and we hope he likes it." Surbhi from Delhi said, "I have been here in Kazan since 2019 and today, we are going to sing a song for PM Modi and we are very excited about that." Parul, a final-year medical student, who has been in Kazan for the last five years told ANI, "We are really grateful that we got this opportunity to welcome our dear Prime Minister." Arti Pawar from Maharashtra said, "I have been living here for the past three years. I am very happy that PM Modi is coming here." Mrunmayi from Nagpur, Maharashtra said, "All the students here are quite enthusiastic as PM is going to come soon. We are too much delighted to welcome him." Meanwhile, ISKCON volunteers - from the Russia n and Indian communities were seen chanting 'Hare Krishna, Hare Ram' ahead of PM Modi 's arrival. While speaking with ANI, Sergoy, an ISKCON volunteer, said, "'Hare Krishna is a Mahamantra. This visit of PM Modi to Kazan , Russia is an important one for us. We are happy." Another ISKCON volunteer said, "We want to welcome PM Modi here in Kazan . It's a great honour for us to welcome him here We are very excited to see him." A Russia n citizen, Alexander said that the people there will welcome PM Modi by singing a song and that he is happy with PM Modi 's visit to Kazan . He said, "We have made a banner and we will also sing a song to welcome PM Modi ... I returned from India just two days back and directly came from Delhi to Kazan to see PM Modi . I am very happy that he is coming to Russia ." Notably, ahead of his departure to Russia , PM Modi shared a post on X and wrote, "Leaving for Kazan , Russia , to take part in the BRICS Summit . India attaches immense importance to BRICS, and I look forward to extensive discussions on a wide range of subjects. I also look forward to meeting various leaders there." The Prime Minister's office in a statement quoted PM Modi as saying, "I am departing today on a two-day visit to Kazan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the Russia n Federation, to attend the 16th BRICS Summit ." "India values the close cooperation within BRICS which has emerged as an important platform for dialogue and discussion on issues concerning the global developmental agenda, reformed multilateralism, climate change, economic cooperation, building resilient supply chains, promoting cultural and people to people connect, among others," PM Modi said. The statement further said that the expansion of BRICS with the addition of new members last year has added to its inclusivity and agenda for the global good. "Building upon the Annual Summit held in July 2024 in Moscow, my visit to Kazan will further reinforce the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia . I look forward to meeting other leaders from BRICS as well," the PMO statement said. The 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan is being held under the chairmanship of Russia from October 22-24. During his visit, PM Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from BRICS member countries and invited leaders in Kazan . The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "The Summit, themed 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security,' will provide an important platform for leaders to discuss key global issues." It further said, "The Summit will offer a valuable opportunity to assess the progress of initiatives launched by BRICS and to identify potential areas for future collaboration." This visit marks, PM Modi 's second visit to Russia this year. He travelled to Moscow in July to attend the 22nd India- Russia Annual Summit where he held a bilateral meeting with President Putin. He was also conferred with Russia 's highest civilian award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle at the Kremlin in Moscow. BRIC, as a formal grouping, started after the meeting of the Leaders of Russia , India and China in St Petersburg on the margins of G8 Outreach Summit in 2006. The grouping was formalized during the first meeting of BRIC Foreign Ministers on the margins of UNGA in New York in 2006. The first BRIC Summit was held in Russia 's Yekaterinburg in 2009. It was agreed to expand BRIC into BRICS with the inclusion of South Africa at the BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting in New York in 2010. South Africa attended the 3rd BRICS Summit in Sanya in 2011. A further expansion of BRICS took place in 2024 with five new members - Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. (ANI)

items.title: "Singapore plays key role in Act-East policy": Rajnath Singh at India-Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Dr. Ng Eng Hen , Singapore 's Minister of Defence , has begun his three-day visit to India . As part of his visit, Dr. Hen co-chaired the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi, with his India n counterpart Rajnath Singh . The Summit began on Tuesday morning, with India n Defence Minister Rajnath Singh welcoming the Singapore delegation warmly. He noted that the strategic partnership the two countries share is a "testimony of increasing closeness between our countries." Singh said, " The meeting is happening at a time when India marks the decade of India 's Act in Policy, in which Singapore has played a key role in promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and developed strategic connectivity with country institutions." Building upon Singh's remarks, Dr. Ng Eng Hen said, "You reminded us that this is the 10th year since your Act East Policy. From Singapore 's perspective, India has always been part of the East. Whether you choose to act or look, we consider you part of the area." He said that while remembering the history of Singapore , India has been an important partner. " When we started the Singapore armed forces, one of the countries that we asked early on to see whether they could help us was India ." Hen highlighted that such historical memoirs serve as important reminders and "reflects how we feel that India is very part of our area. We are delighted that our ten years of bilateral relations have been very much improved in defence and all-round strategic partnership." Hen also thanked PM Modi for visiting Singapore earlier this year and noted that the visit was an excellent meeting. A day before, the Ministry of Defence had announced the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi on October 22, 2024. The release noted that between India and Singapore , "The engagements have diversified to include wide-ranging contacts between the Services, military-to-military exchanges, high-level visits, capacity building and training programs, cooperation in UN Peacekeeping, ship visits and bilateral exercises." Inaugurated in 2016, the India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue is a key platform to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation between Singapore and India . The fifth edition of the Defence Ministers' Dialogue took place in January 2021 through virtual teleconference. During the meeting, the two parties showed confidence in the outcomes of the meeting that would result in providing impetus to the entire spectrum of the bilateral engagement as well as to the regional security architecture. (ANI)

items.title: "India matters most for future of planet" says British High Commissioner Lindy Cameron
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): In recent times when climate change has become a pressing issue with countries across the world being ravaged due to climate catastrophes, it becomes imperative to discuss and deliberate upon global actions that can help the world rise up and meet these challenges. At the NDTV World Summit's a discussion was held on the theme, "India Matters The Most For Future Of Planet". Participants in the discussion included Erik Solheim, Former Minister of Climate and the Environment of Norway; Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India; Shishir Priyadarshi, President Chintan Research Foundation; Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative. "India is the country that matters the most for the future of the planet and climate change. India's ambition for development should not in any way be constrained by the responsibilities of the planet," Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India, emphasised. She noted that the UK is committed towards the Multilateral Development Banks (MDB) reforms, technology and research support in India to aid the efforts. "Every dollar invested in resilient infrastructure pays 4 times over," said Cameron. "Lived experience of climate emergencies helps people to understand why their government needs to take policy action now," she added. Further talking about the need for urgent government action, Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative said, "Series of disasters affecting both developed and developing countries are serving as a wake-up call. As rich countries will get more and more affected by climate change which they did not imagine till a couple of years ago, most vulnerable countries are going to be struggling with impacts who also have very less capacity to deal with it. India is taking a leadership role in the global fight against climate change. Initiatives such as Global Biofuels Alliance, International Solar Alliance, and Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure are some efforts taken by India in recent years to manage the climate crisis. (ANI)

items.title: "No shortage of oil in world and prices should hopefully come down", says Hardeep Singh Puri
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Hardeep Singh Puri, Minister for Petroleum and Natural Gas on Tuesday said that there is no shortage of oil in the world and prices will come down soon, answering the question of the recent upswing in crude oil prices. Speaking to the media, the Union Minister cited global factors such as the war in the Middle East and voluntary cuts in oil production which are influencing the oil prices in the global market. He said, "It depends on global factors. One thing is very clear, there is no shortage of oil in the world...Today, more and more oil is coming on the market...There are other factors like geopolitical tensions. So, there is no shortage of oil but if there is tension in one part of the world, then the freight cost, and insurance freight cost will go up. Today, let us all hope that better sense prevails, that call for peace that our Prime Minister has been making from every forum...There is more than enough oil in the world and prices should hopefully come down. That's my expectation..." "If there's tension in one part of the world, then the cost of, if you have to take a longer route, then the cost of the freight cost, the insurance rate cost, that will go up...There's more than enough oil in the world, and prices should hopefully come down," he commented in his personal capacity.

The union minister said many countries such as Brazil, and Guayana among others are coming with their oil. Citing the stable prices in the last 3 years, the minister said that the government is taking every possible step to ensure stable oil prices. "Central government at every stage has stepped in to cushion and bring the prices down from November 2021 to May 2022. Now there are some global factors. The cost at the retail point is determined by the cost of the barrel in the international market plus the cost of transportation, freight, insurance, retailers, refining cost and margin, then dealers, margin, etc. We are solving all the problems we can, now you tell the global community to hold and bring them down," he added. This comes after oil prices rose nearly 2 per cent on Monday, reclaiming major losses from last week's sell-off. Brent crude features upped by $1.44, or 1.97 per cent in the afternoon. Earlier this month, Puri had said that the country is well-prepared to meet its growing energy demands, with a diverse range of oil sources. Speaking on the availability of oil in the global market, Puri emphasised that India has expanded its procurement base, moving from 27 suppliers to 39. (ANI)

items.title: India is the top market for investment globally: Mark Mobius
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Mark Mobius, Founder of Mobius Capital Partners LLP , and an ace investor with expertise in emerging markets said, India's is the top stock market globally where he would like to invest. In an exclusive interview with ANI, the octagenarian said, "India would have to come first when I think about investment," Mobius stated, "Of course, India would have to be the first choice. Then, I would probably look at Taiwan. It's a Chinese society, but it's a free society and they're doing very well. Now we're beginning to see China rise again. There will be some interesting companies in China, but still, India remains our top pick." Mobius highlighted technology as his favorite sector to invest in India. "In the future, I believe there's going to be significant growth in hardware technology. As you know, India is already strong in software technology, but moving forward, hardware manufacturing will gain momentum here in India," he said. Discussing India's semiconductor infrastructure, Mobius mentioned that it is already developing. "Many of the world's large semiconductor companies already have software development operations in India, employing thousands of software engineers. The next step, of course, is hardware. Soon, we'll see large semiconductor manufacturing plants. The scale of investment we're talking about isn't in the millions, but billions of dollars, to produce the most advanced semiconductors in the world." Mobius also fondly remembered Ratan Tata, who passed away this month. "I met him many years ago and found him to be a very friendly, humble, and insightful person. I was deeply saddened to hear about his passing. I considered him one of the great Indian entrepreneurs of the century," Mobius added. Earlier on Monday, Mark Mobius, speaking at the NDTV World Summit 2024, reiterated he was bullish on India's real estate and semiconductor sectors, as he outlined the potential of these two key industries. In the semiconductor space, he said fabrication companies (fabs) will come here because India has got the population and the labour force. The octagenarian believes India will become "the leader" of the semiconductor industry. The government has so far approved five semiconductor units in India, of which construction in two sites is on, and soon the work in the other three will start. The companies have already made a cumulative investment of almost Rs 1.5 lakh crore. While talking about the parameters he looks at while investing in companies, Mobius said he looks at the growth of earnings in companies, along with the return on capital invested, and the quality of management. Asked about his investment advice to his "younger self," Mobius said, "Don't be in a rush, and study carefully". He added that one has to listen to the market. (ANI)

items.title: Jodar confirms Davis Cup Final 8 with Spain: “Something unique”
paras: After his opening loss at the ATP Finals in Turin, the Spaniard said he will have little time to rest: Spain comes next, then a one-month break to prepare 2027 “without any expectations”. Rafael Jodar will play the Davis Cup Final 8 with Spain next week, straight after the ATP Finals.

The 8th seed confirmed it in Turin on Sunday, after his 6-4, 6-4 loss to Alexander Zverev in his first ever ATP Finals match. “I still have this tournament and next week, Davis Cup as well,” Jodar said in his press conference.

Italy, the defending champion, hosts the Davis Cup by Generali Final 8 in Bologna from November 24 to 29. After the Davis Cup, he plans to take a break. “I’ll have one month to prepare for the next season and without any expectations, trying to go tournament by tournament, knowing that the year is very long,” he explained.

items.title: How Aryna Sabalenka’s record and prize money from the 2026 WTA season compares to 2025
paras: After losing the Australian Open final to Elena Rybakina , the former world number one bounced back emphatically, winning Indian Wells and the Miami Open.
At the time, it seemed the Belarusian would go on to dominate proceedings on the WTA Tour throughout 2026.

Sabalenka went on to suffer a plethora of early exits at significant WTA Tour events: including a concerning defeat to Diana Shnaider at the French Open , and a worrisome performance against Jessica Pegula in Berlin. Sabalenka has done little to improve her situation since the summer , and has now fallen to world number three for the first time since August 12, 2024. Sabalenka enjoyed an excellent campaign on the WTA Tour, winning one Grand Slam title – the US Open – and maintaining her number one ranking throughout the entire year.

items.title: ATP Finals Day 2 Predictions Including Carlos Alcaraz vs Frances Tiafoe
paras: As always, we here at LWOT will be offering our predictions for both matches on day two at the Palasport Olimpico. But who will claim a vital win as the Ivan Lendl Group gets underway?

It has been a challenging season for Carlos Alcaraz as the Spaniard has faced disruptive injury issues for the first time in his young career. But he still won the Australian Open and comes into the ATP Finals in form after lifting the Vienna Open and the Paris Masters titles.

If he can maintain the form he showed in the Austrian and the French capitals, he will surely have a real shot at winning the season-ending championships for the first time in his career. But he will need to be at his best up against Frances Tiafoe, a player who has given him real trouble in the past.

items.title: Jessica Pegula suggests the main reason why she lost to Mirra Andreeva at the WTA Finals
paras: Jessica Pegula has exited the WTA Finals after a semifinal defeat to Mirra Andreeva. Andreeva surprised herself against Pegula , who she beat 6-3, 6-4 after one hour and 25 minutes.
Despite the superb victory, Andreeva still doesn’t understand how Pegula plays . But that matters not right now as the Russian teenager turns her focus to her experienced WTA rival Elina Svitolina.

They will meet in the final of the WTA Finals , having already played against each other in the group stage. Meanwhile, Pegula has been left wondering what could have been at Indian Wells, where the crowd were eager to see a home favourite emerge. But the American has fallen short, and has since suggested the main reason behind her exit. Speaking after losing to Andreeva, Pegula said: “Yeah, I mean I didn’t think I had a good serving day.

items.title: Alexander Zverev sends statement to his rivals in his first match at the ATP Finals with Rafael Jodar
paras: Alexander Zverev opened his 2026 ATP Finals campaign with victory on Sunday afternoon. The new world number one wasted little time stamping his mark on the competition, beating young starlet Rafael Jodar 6-4, 6-4 in one hour and 27 minutes.

Zverev , who is looking to win his third ATP Finals title at this year’s event, will look to strengthen his chances of reaching the semi-finals in Turin when he plays Ben Shelton and Arthur Fils later this week. Zverev was certainly in fine form against Jodar – his rivals should be concerned after witnessing the German’s serving prowess against the young Spaniard.
If Zverev continues to serve as he did against Jodar, he will be the frontrunner for the 2026 title. How long do you think Alexander Zverev keeps the number one ranking?

Friendships are built by repeated contact, not by being liked
items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
items.do: Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800.
